title: Episode 118: James Monroe and the Monroe Doctrine: Drawing the Line in the Western Hemisphere
description:
In eighteen twenty-three, the global political landscape was convulsed by revolutionary change. Across South and Central America, the once-mighty Spanish Empire was crumbling. Revolutionary heroes like Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín had defeated Spanish royalist armies, giving birth to a constellation of newborn republics in Mexico, Colombia, Chile, and Argentina. The United States had proudly become the first nation to officially recognize these independent sister republics.

Yet across the Atlantic, the victorious monarchs of Europe were determined to turn back the clock of history. Under the banner of the Holy Alliance, the autocratic rulers of Russia, Prussia, Austria, and France banded together to crush democratic revolutions wherever they sparked. Having crushed rebellions in Naples and Spain, rumors swirled that the Alliance was preparing a massive expeditionary armada to reconquer Latin America for the Spanish crown. Simultaneously, Czar Alexander I of Russia issued an imperial ukase declaring the Pacific coast of North America down to the fifty-first parallel closed to foreign shipping.

British Foreign Secretary George Canning proposed that Great Britain and the United States issue a joint declaration opposing French intervention. Elder statesmen Thomas Jefferson and James Madison urged President James Monroe to accept the British offer. But Secretary of State John Quincy Adams fiercely disagreed, arguing that America should act independently rather than 'come in as a cockboat in the wake of the British man-of-war.' Monroe sided with Adams, drafting a bold, unilateral declaration in his Seventh Annual Message to Congress that established the cornerstone of American foreign policy for two centuries: The Monroe Doctrine. Here is the story of the day America drew a line in the ocean and told the empires of Europe to stand down.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we meet our fifth President, James Monroe, the last of the Virginia Dynasty and the final president of the Revolutionary generation. Monroe was a battlefield veteran who had been severely wounded crossing the Delaware with George Washington at Trenton. By eighteen twenty-three, the world was at a perilous crossroads. Across Latin America, new republics had broken free from Spain, but an autocratic coalition of European emperors known as the Holy Alliance was plotting to crush them. In a moment of supreme geopolitical audacity, President Monroe issued a decree that reshaped world history. Here is George with the story of the Monroe Doctrine.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CRUMBLING EMPIRE OF SPAIN
By eighteen twenty-two, the geopolitical map of the Western Hemisphere was undergoing a seismic transformation. For three centuries, the Spanish Crown had held vast territories stretching from California and Texas all the way to the southern tip of Cape Horn. But the Napoleonic Wars in Europe had decapitated Spanish authority, igniting ferocious wars of liberation across Latin America. Brilliant libertadores like Simón Bolívar in the north and José de San Martín in the south led ragged, determined armies across the frozen Andes, smashing royalist legions and establishing independent republics in Venezuela, Colombia, Peru, Chile, and Argentina. In eighteen twenty-one, Mexico also declared its independence, ending three hundred years of colonial rule.
In the United States, these revolutions were greeted with intense popular enthusiasm. Americans saw in the Latin American struggles a mirror of their own revolution of seventeen seventy-six. Henry Clay, the fiery Speaker of the House, delivered passionate orations demanding that the United States formally recognize these new sister republics. President James Monroe and his brilliant Secretary of State, John Quincy Adams, moved with calculated deliberation. Once the Adams-Onís Treaty was finalized—securing the peaceful cession of Florida from Spain to the United States—Monroe officially recognized the independence of Colombia, Mexico, Chile, and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata in eighteen twenty-two, making America the first nation in the world to do so.
Yet this triumph of liberty was desperately fragile. The infant republics were economically devastated, politically fractured, and completely lacking naval forces. And across the Atlantic, the crowned monarchs of Europe viewed the emergence of republican democracies in the Americas with absolute horror.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MENACE OF THE HOLY ALLIANCE
In the aftermath of Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo, the reactionary monarchs of Europe formed a mutual protection pact known as the Holy Alliance. Spearheaded by Czar Alexander I of Russia, Emperor Francis I of Austria, and King Frederick William III of Prussia, and later joined by the restored Bourbon monarchy of France, the Alliance dedicated itself to upholding the divine right of kings and eradicating democratic revolutions wherever they arose.
The Holy Alliance was not an idle diplomatic forum; it was an armed counter-revolutionary syndicate. In eighteen twenty-one, Austrian troops marched into Italy to crush constitutional uprisings in Naples and Piedmont. In eighteen twenty-three, with the blessing of the Alliance, a French army of one hundred thousand soldiers invaded Spain, overthrew the liberal constitutional government in Madrid, and restored the autocratic King Ferdinand VII to absolute power. Having secured Spain, rumors spread across European capitals that the Holy Alliance was planning its next move: dispatching a joint Franco-Spanish fleet to reconquer Latin America and carve up the former colonies among the European monarchies.
Simultaneously, Czar Alexander of Russia made an alarming imperial move in North America. In September eighteen twenty-one, the Czar issued an imperial ukase claiming Russian sovereignty over the Pacific Northwest down to the fifty-first parallel—modern-day British Columbia—and prohibiting foreign ships from approaching within one hundred miles of the coast. The young American republic found itself caught in a tightening vice between Russian autocracy in the northwest and monarchical intervention in the south.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BRITISH PROPOSAL: TRAP OR SHIELD?
Into this combustible crisis stepped Great Britain. Britain had broken with the Holy Alliance, having no desire to see a French-dominated Bourbon alliance control the vast wealth of the Americas. British merchants had developed lucrative, booming trade ties with the newly independent Latin American republics, and the restoration of the Spanish colonial monopoly would devastate British commerce.
In August eighteen twenty-three, British Foreign Secretary George Canning approached the American minister in London, Richard Rush, with an extraordinary confidential proposal. Canning proposed that Great Britain and the United States issue a joint public declaration. The declaration would state that neither nation sought to acquire any portion of Spain's former colonies, but that neither would permit any other European power to intervene or subjugate the new republics.
When Rush's dispatches reached Washington in October, President James Monroe was deeply tempted. Great Britain possessed the Royal Navy, the undisputed master of the global oceans. A joint declaration with the world's greatest naval superpower would immediately deter France, Russia, and the Holy Alliance. Monroe sent the confidential documents to his two living predecessors, Thomas Jefferson and James Madison, seeking their counsel.
Both elder statesmen urged Monroe to accept the British offer. Jefferson, writing from Monticello at age eighty, noted that while America's first fundamental rule was never to entangle herself in the broils of Europe, her second rule was never to suffer Europe to meddle in cis-Atlantic affairs. Jefferson wrote that with Great Britain on America's side, 'we need not fear the whole world.' Madison agreed, urging an even broader declaration that championed liberty worldwide. Monroe prepared to accept the joint British pact. But one man in the cabinet stood stubbornly, fiercely against it.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: JOHN QUINCY ADAMS AND THE COCKBOAT PRINCIPLE
That lone dissenting voice belonged to Secretary of State John Quincy Adams. The son of John Adams, John Quincy was the most experienced diplomat in American history, having served in embassies across Europe since his teenage years. Adams possessed a keen, razor-sharp understanding of European imperial motives, and he saw right through George Canning's proposal.
In a series of intense, dramatic cabinet debates throughout November eighteen twenty-three, Adams argued passionately against a joint declaration. First, Adams pointed out that Canning's proposal bound the United States never to acquire any former Spanish territory. While Britain already had a vast global empire, such a pledge would prevent the natural expansion of the United States into neighboring lands like Texas or Cuba, which might one day voluntarily seek to join the American union.
Second, and most fundamentally, Adams argued that issuing a joint statement with Great Britain would make the United States look weak, subservient, and cowardly. Britain had not even formally recognized the independence of the Latin American republics, as America had done. In a line that became legendary in the annals of American statecraft, Adams told the cabinet: 'It would be more candid, as well as more dignified, to avow our principles explicitly to Russia and France, than to come in as a cockboat in the wake of the British man-of-war.'
Adams argued that the United States must have the courage to stand on its own feet. The British navy would protect Latin American trade for its own commercial self-interest regardless of whether America signed a treaty. Therefore, America should issue a unilateral, independent declaration of principles, proclaiming to the world that the Western Hemisphere was no longer open to European conquest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SEVENTH ANNUAL MESSAGE TO CONGRESS
President James Monroe listened carefully to the conflicting counsel of his mentors Jefferson and Madison on one side, and his brilliant Secretary of State on the other. In the end, Monroe embraced Adams's audacious vision. Rather than issuing a diplomatic note or signing a treaty with Britain, Monroe decided to embed the policy directly into his Seventh Annual Message to Congress on December second, eighteen twenty-three.
Delivered as a written message read aloud to Congress, the doctrine was articulated in two crucial passages. Addressing the Russian claims in the Pacific Northwest, Monroe stated unequivocally: 'The American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.'
Turning to the Holy Alliance and the threat to Latin America, Monroe drew a bright, uncrossable line in the sand. He declared that the political system of the European monarchies was essentially different from that of America, and that any attempt on their part to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere would be considered 'as dangerous to our peace and safety.' Monroe affirmed that the United States would not interfere with existing European colonies, nor would it take part in the internal wars of European nations. But regarding the newly liberated republics: 'We could not view any interposition for the purpose of oppressing them, or controlling in any other manner their destiny, by any European power in any other light than as the manifestation of an unfriendly disposition toward the United States.'
It was a breathtaking assertion of hemispheric authority by a nation of barely ten million people, possessing a peacetime army of fewer than six thousand soldiers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE GLOBAL SHOCKWAVE
Monroe's message detonated across the capitals of Europe like a diplomatic thunderclap. In Paris, Vienna, and Saint Petersburg, autocratic rulers reacted with incredulous indignation. Prince Klemens von Metternich, the powerful Austrian chancellor who orchestrated the Holy Alliance, dismissed the doctrine with aristocratic sneers, calling it an 'indecent, arrogant declaration' that demonstrated the 'revolutionary insolence' of the American republic. Czar Alexander of Russia grumbled that the Americans were daring to lecture the crowned heads of the earth.
In London, George Canning was privately furious that the Americans had stolen his diplomatic thunder and issued a unilateral doctrine without British co-authorship. Yet Canning also recognized that Monroe had achieved Britain's primary commercial objective: warning off France and Russia. Backed by the silent, formidable deterrent of the British fleet and Monroe's explicit warning, the Holy Alliance abandoned any plans for an armed expedition to the Americas. The French troops remained in Spain, and within months, Russia signed a treaty with the United States agreeing to limit its claims in the Pacific Northwest to the fifty-four-forty parallel.
Across Latin America, the reaction was one of gratitude and relief. Simón Bolívar hailed the United States for its solidarity, and the congresses of Colombia and Argentina praised the declaration as a magnificent gesture of republican fraternity. Though the phrase 'The Monroe Doctrine' would not be coined until three decades later, the principle was permanently established: the Americas were a separate hemisphere dedicated to self-determination and closed forever to colonial conquest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: TWO CENTURIES OF HEMISPHERIC SHIELD
In the decades that followed, the Monroe Doctrine evolved from an audacious presidential statement into the bedrock foundation of American grand strategy. While critics in later eras noted that the doctrine was occasionally repurposed by later administrations to justify American interventions in the Caribbean, its primary, enduring purpose remained unchanged: preventing hostile foreign powers from establishing military footholds on the American continent.
During the American Civil War, when Emperor Napoleon III of France took advantage of the conflict to install the Austrian Archduke Maximilian as puppet Emperor of Mexico, Secretary of State William Seward invoked the Monroe Doctrine the moment the Civil War ended. Moving fifty thousand veteran Union troops to the Rio Grande under General Phil Sheridan, the United States forced France to withdraw its legions, leaving the Mexican people to restore their sovereign republic under Benito Juárez.
A century later, during the harrowing Cuban Missile Crisis of nineteen sixty-two, President John F. Kennedy invoked the core principle of Monroe's message, establishing a naval quarantine to force the Soviet Union to remove nuclear missiles from the Western Hemisphere.
James Monroe was the last president of the revolutionary generation, the final soldier of Washington's army to hold the highest office. In crafting the Monroe Doctrine, he left his country an enduring shield. He demonstrated that true national greatness does not lie in conforming to the old rules of empires, but in having the courage to establish new standards of freedom, sovereignty, and independence for the entire world.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Monroe Doctrine transformed a young, untested republic into the diplomatic protector of a new hemisphere. James Monroe and John Quincy Adams proved that moral clarity and strategic independence could stand down the combined empires of Europe. Next week, we explore James Monroe's domestic legacy: the fabled Era of Good Feelings, and the epic engineering feat of the Cumberland Road, the first great federal highway that breached the Appalachian mountains and unlocked the American West. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
